title: Hyderabad-Born MIT Astronomer Rohan Naidu Helps Discover a 'Black Hole Star'
excerpt: The Pappalardo Fellow at MIT led a Nature study identifying MoM-BH*-1, an extraordinary object from the early universe that could reshape understanding of how supermassive black holes formed.
body:
• Rohan Naidu, a Hyderabad-born astrophysicist at MIT, led a team that identified MoM-BH*-1 — a possible "black hole star" from the early universe — in a study published in Nature.
  • The object, roughly the size of our solar system and 100 billion times brighter than an ordinary star, may contain a black hole 100,000 times the mass of the Sun buried inside a dense hydrogen envelope.
  • The discovery could explain the mysterious "little red dots" that the James Webb Space Telescope has been spotting across the early universe.

A Hyderabad-born astronomer at MIT has helped identify what could be an entirely new class of cosmic object — a "black hole star" from the early universe that challenges existing models of how supermassive black holes grew so massive, so fast.

Rohan Naidu, a Pappalardo Fellow at MIT's Kavli Institute for Astrophysics and Space Research, is the lead author of the study, published in Nature. The discovery was made using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and could have far-reaching implications for understanding the universe's formative years.

An Object Like No Other

The object, designated MoM-BH*-1, was found during the Mirage or Miracle (MoM) survey, which uses JWST to search for some of the earliest and most distant galaxies in the universe. Researchers noticed a source that was exceptionally bright and unusually red — characteristics that did not fit any known type of star or galaxy.

https://x.com/dna/status/2089332814433173899

According to the Times of India, scientists believe MoM-BH*-1 may contain a central black hole roughly 100,000 times the mass of the Sun, surrounded by an enormous envelope of dense hydrogen extending to approximately the scale of our solar system. The resulting structure is about 100 billion times brighter than an ordinary star.

"It is a very special thing to find an object with no comparison given the vast stores of data on billions of stars, galaxies, and black holes that we have in our archival databases. MoM-BH*-1 is one in a billion!"

— Rohan Naidu, MIT

The object was so luminous that it outshone its entire host galaxy, allowing researchers to study the black-hole-star-like component without having to separate it from the fainter glow of surrounding stars, according to the New York Post.

How a 'Black Hole Star' Works

The term describes a proposed configuration rather than a conventional star. As matter falls toward an actively feeding black hole, gravitational energy is converted into vast amounts of radiation — far greater than what ordinary stars generate through nuclear fusion.

In MoM-BH*-1, the dense hydrogen surrounding the black hole may be so thick that the entire structure takes on a star-like appearance from the outside. The black hole provides the engine; the hydrogen envelope determines how that energy appears from a distance, according to the Times of India.

The researchers found further clues in the object's spectrum, including an unusually deep Balmer break — a feature associated with hydrogen absorbing particular wavelengths of light. The observations also showed little evidence of heavier elements, consistent with the early universe before repeated generations of stars had enriched cosmic gas with metals.

Solving the Mystery of the 'Little Red Dots'

The discovery carries significance well beyond a single unusual object. Since JWST began observing the early universe, astronomers have found numerous compact sources that appear unusually red. These have been dubbed "little red dots," and their true nature remains one of the telescope's most debated puzzles.

Naidu's finding suggests that at least some of these objects could be black hole stars — black holes surrounded by dense gas that radiate in a manner reminiscent of stellar phenomena. MoM-BH*-1's red appearance may be the result of gas rather than dust, which could help explain why the earliest supermassive black holes grew far bigger than cosmological models predict, according to the New York Post.

From Hyderabad to the Edge of Cosmic History

Naidu's path to this discovery is almost as unconventional as the object itself. According to his MIT biography, he grew up in Hyderabad and initially studied engineering. At 18, he dropped out, bought his first-ever plane ticket, and traveled to Singapore to join the founding class of Yale-NUS College.

It was there that his interest in astronomy took root. He subsequently worked on blazars in the Chilean Andes and gained research experience with astronomers including Iva Momcheva and Pascal Oesch, according to the Times of India. He later pursued a PhD at Harvard under Professor Charlie Conroy, studying the ancient history of the Milky Way, before his research shifted to the earliest galaxies and black holes that formed after the Big Bang.

What's Next

MoM-BH*-1 remains a candidate, not a confirmed new class of object. Further observations will be needed to determine whether the black hole star interpretation holds up to scrutiny.

Starting in December, Naidu and his team plan to use JWST to probe further, examining the object's actual size and the composition of its atmosphere. "Our picture of this object is evolving very rapidly," Naidu said, according to Nature.

If black hole stars existed in large numbers in the early universe, they could help explain how the enormous supermassive black holes found at the centers of modern galaxies came into existence — a question that has puzzled astronomers for decades.
